We jointly learn the predictor and a positive-definite mobility, adapting the correction geometry to improve objective quality. We prove convergence of the outer iterates at fixed dual depth and linear convergence in distance under Slater's condition and bounded subgradients. All our test outputs on three second-order-cone model-predictive control (SOC-MPC) horizons and six power-system convex relaxations satisfy a $10^{-3}$ feasibility tolerance. Comparisons with the latest constraint-satisfaction methods show inference speedups of up to $144.3\times$ on SOC-MPC and $7.7\times$ on a convex quadratically constrained quadratic programming (QCQP) benchmark with joint training. On QCQP, the mean objective gap is $0.012\%$, with full test feasibility at $10^{-4}$. Learning mobility reduces the five-seed affine-task mean gap by $22.4\%$ and improves gaps in matched power-system comparisons.
item.dc:creator: Haoyu Zhu, Xiaochen Zhang, Qingchun Hou

item.title: Damped stochastic mirror descent for non-smooth ill-posed problems in Banach space
item.description: arXiv:2610.38258v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We introduce a damped variant of the stochastic mirror descent method for systems of non-smooth nonlinear ill-posed operator equations in Banach spaces. At each iteration, the method samples a random subset of the equations, performs a mirror-descent step in the dual space with an adaptive step size derived from the discrepancy principle, and applies a damping term that prevents the iterates from drifting away from the initial guess. The scheme accommodates non-smooth forward operators through a family of bounded linear surrogates, admits general $p$-convex penalty functionals which also includes trained convex penalty, allows the noise level to differ from equation to equation, and dispenses with two classical requirements, namely reflexivity of the image space and G\^ateaux differentiability of the forward operator. We study its regularization properties under an \textit{a posteriori} stopping rule by proving first that the iteration terminates after finitely many steps almost surely, and then that the mean-square error of the iterates tends to zero as the noise level vanishes. Numerical experiments on a system of non-smooth semilinear inverse source problems and the identification of a diffusion coefficient confirm the theoretical analysis and shows improved convergence results.
item.dc:creator: Harshit Bajpai, Gaurav Mittal, Ankik Kumar Giri

item.title: Game-Theoretic Foundations for Undiscounted Bisimulation Metrics
item.description: arXiv:2610.38313v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Bisimulation metrics offer a principled notion of task-relevant state similarity in reinforcement learning, but existing constructions and methods are largely confined to discounted MDPs, where contraction arguments ensure well-defined fixed points and downstream guarantees. We develop a unified foundation for bisimulation metrics in undiscounted settings, that is total- and average-reward problems, by replacing the standard operator-centric view with a game-centric one: we interpret prior metric operators as Bellman-Shapley operators of zero-sum turn-based games and define metrics as the corresponding game value functions, yielding unique definitions even when $\gamma=1$. This game-theoretic foundation facilitates transfer of dynamic-programming theory and algorithms. We also use this game-centric perspective to characterize how metric finiteness depends on structural properties of the underlying MDP and motivate certain directed metrics that remain finite in weakly communicating MDPs. We further introduce an abstract framework for modifying the games' action spaces, allowing general transition coupling sets, that recovers many existing metrics and guides new constructions. Finally, we prove that these metrics bound total-reward and, when the optimal gain is state-independent, optimal relative value differences. We also provide error and suboptimality guarantees for aggregation-based planning in total- and average-reward settings.
item.dc:creator: Matthew Zurek, Yudong Chen, Josiah P. Hanna

item.title: Controllability-Based Input Allocation in Quantum System
item.description: arXiv:2610.38415v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Understanding how local perturbations influence global quantum dynamics is important for analyzing and designing large-scale quantum systems. Existing quantum centrality measures often rely on static correlations or entanglement and do not directly capture perturbation propagation under unitary evolution. We formulate controllability allocation scoring for quantum input-output dynamics governed by the Schrodinger equation. Using the multiobservable quantum-control Gramian, we introduce virtual local Hamiltonian perturbations along a nominal trajectory and decompose the terminal-output response into channel-wise Gramian contributions. A simplex-constrained log-determinant optimization combines these contributions to define a volumetric controllability allocation score (V-CAS), specifying an optimal allocation of virtual input intensities among local Hamiltonian perturbation directions. The score measures their cooperative dynamical influence and depends on the output and trajectory. We characterize the output Gramian's range and minimum-energy properties and derive a drift-independent sufficient condition ensuring score uniqueness for almost every terminal time at which the problem is feasible. For quantum many-body systems, we develop a matrix-product-state and time-evolving-block-decimation implementation that avoids explicitly constructing exponentially large state-transition matrices. We also derive an error bound propagating Trotter and MPS-truncation errors to the discrete output Gramian. Numerical experiments show that the score captures finite-time influence patterns distinct from those identified by static correlation- and entanglement-based measures and can inform target-independent control-channel preselection.
item.dc:creator: Riku Yaegashi, Kazuhiro Sato, Kentaro Ohki

item.title: Carnot geodesics with H\"older controls
item.description: arXiv:2610.38481v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We construct an explicit length-minimizing curve in a polynomial rank-two sub-Riemannian structure on $\R^4$. Its arclength parametrization is $C^{1,1/2}$ and is not $C^{1,\alpha}$ near an interior point for any $\alpha>1/2$. Minimality is proved by an approximate calibration chosen separately for each competitor. The example admits a minimizing lift to a rank-two Carnot group of step five. Generalizations are announced.
item.dc:creator: Nicola Cavallucci, Enrico Le Donne, Sebastiano Nicolussi Golo

item.title: Accelerating Nonlinear MPC by Behavior Cloning with Separated Timescales: Application to Nuclear Reactor Load-Following
item.description: arXiv:2610.38496v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Behavior Cloning (BC) of expert controllers for multiscale dynamical systems is challenging: state variables evolving at widely separated timescales induce highly nonlinear couplings that a shared latent space may fail to adequately represent, degrading closed-loop generalization. We propose Structured Representation Learning for Behavior Cloning (SRLBC), an architecture designed to leverage the physical knowledge of multiscale systems in which slow state variables, fast (stiff) state variables, and predictable exogenous inputs evolve at different timescales. On 500 long-horizon roll-outs of a pressurized water reactor (PWR) load-following benchmark -a high-dimensional, stiff industrial system with challenging safety constraints -and across 20 training seeds, separated embeddings systematically outperform shared embedding baselines on cumulative cost, imitation accuracy and constraint satisfaction. The resulting standalone policies approach NMPC closed-loop performance at a computational cost 15 times lower on average. Since standalone policies still leave a few percent of trajectories infeasible, we embed the learned policies in a safety-augmented approximate NMPC framework, in which the optimizer is only called when the predicted input sequence is not certified as safe. This yields controllers still 6.8 times faster than the NMPC controller on average, with a feasibility (i.e., constraint satisfaction) of at least 99.8% for all architectures, SRLBC retaining the lowest closed-loop cost. Under distribution shift, standalone BC policies degrade sharply: SRLBC degrades the least, and once safety-augmented, it retains a feasibility above 98% with the lowest closed-loop cost. Beyond the quantitative results, Jacobian-based sensitivity analysis shows that the resulting controller relies on a sparse and less redundant set of latent features, each attributable to a single group of physical variables, and aligned with the physical timescale decomposition of the system.
item.dc:creator: Perceval Beja-Battais (CB), Alain Grosset{\^e}te (CB), Nicolas Vayatis (CB)

item.title: The Power Watershed as a Differentiable Segmentation Layer
item.description: arXiv:2610.38516v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Can a Watershed transform, the classical tool of morphological segmentation, be placed at the end of a deep network and trained through? The Power Watershed (PW) is the limit of the seeded Random Walker (RW) as p grows to infinity with edge weights raised to the power p. At every finite p the RW solves a sparse positive-definite linear system and is exactly differentiable with respect to the edge weights and the unaries through one adjoint solve; its multi-label form costs one right-hand side per label, and its limit is the PW. We study this family as the last layer of a segmentation network, the watershed layer (WS layer). A conditioning study measures how the solve, the gradient and the distance to the limit evolve with p, and the implicit gradient is checked against unrolling. On synthetic data with correct edge costs the WS layer transforms a soft prediction into an exact boundary. On nuclei segmentation (PanNuke), a binary WS layer is level with a thresholded U-Net. With the instances as labels, the WS layer turns the U-Net into an instance segmenter whose number of labels is set per image by the markers rather than by the output layout, and the network is trained through that partition: instance F1 score rises from 0.656 to 0.795 over a U-Net with connected components, level with the same network followed by a tuned marker watershed. At the training temperature the partition is a watershed of the learned costs, and the finite temperature lets the solve hedge, discounting weak markers and sharing contested pixels. The hedging puts the WS layer 0.015--0.020 F1 ahead of the baseline when trained on a tenth of the data, at the price of having to deploy the finite-p solve rather than its exact limit at inference. Code and the full experimental record are released.
item.dc:creator: Galia Akl (AUB), Laurent Najman (LIGM, KUSTAR), Hugues Talbot (OPIS, CVN)

item.title: Rennala NSGD: Asynchronous Stochastic Optimization Beyond Euclidean Geometry
item.description: arXiv:2610.38773v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The empirical success of matrix-aware optimizers, such as Muon (Jordan et al., 2024) and Shampoo (arXiv:1802.09568), highlights the potential of non-Euclidean geometry for deep learning, including large language model (LLM) training. Despite this progress, the theoretical understanding of stochastic optimization in general normed spaces remains limited, particularly in distributed settings. We analyze minibatch stochastic gradient descent (SGD) for smooth nonconvex optimization with respect to an arbitrary norm on a finite-dimensional space. Using the framework of $\kappa$-regular normed spaces (arXiv:0809.0813), we derive high-probability oracle complexity bounds under a light-tail condition stated directly in the dual norm induced by the update norm. The bounds make the dependence on geometry explicit through the regularity constant $\kappa$ of the dual space. In the Euclidean case, our bound recovers the standard minibatch SGD rate up to logarithmic factors. For some non-Euclidean geometries and noise models, it is sharper than bounds obtained by converting a Euclidean noise assumption, reducing a linear dimension dependence to a logarithmic one. Building on this framework, we introduce Rennala NSGD, a semi-asynchronous distributed algorithm, and establish wall-clock time complexity guarantees under fixed, heterogeneous worker computation times. In the Euclidean case ($\kappa=1$), our bound matches the parameter dependence of classical Rennala SGD up to logarithmic factors.
item.dc:creator: Igor Sokolov, Alexander Tyurin, Peter Richt\'arik

item.title: Controllability of Nonlocal Partial Differential Equations
item.description: arXiv:2610.38933v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This chapter provides a short survey of recent developments in the controllability of nonlocal partial differential equations. We first review controllability results for evolution equations involving nonlocal spatial operators. Particular attention is devoted to unique continuation properties, observability inequalities, and Carleman estimates in establishing controllability properties. We then discuss controllability issues for partial differential equations with memory terms, highlighting how memory effects influence reachable states, null controllability, and exact controllability. We review and compare various analytical techniques developed to overcome the difficulties arising from the nonlocal structure. We also provide a critical assessment of some of these methods. Throughout the chapter, we emphasize the interplay between controllability and observability, the adaptation of classical control methods to nonlocal settings, and the distinctive phenomena that arise in comparison with local equations. We then discuss geometric inequalities and their role in the controllability of diffusion models. The chapter concludes with a discussion of current challenges and several open problems, aiming to provide directions for future research.
item.dc:creator: D. Cardona, S. E. Chorfi, F. Et-tahri, L. Maniar

item.title: Topology and regularity of small sub-Riemannian balls under an index condition
item.description: arXiv:2610.38962v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study the topology and regularity of small sub-Riemannian balls under an index condition on length-minimizing curves in the metric tangent space. We prove that sufficiently small spheres are Lipschitz hypersurfaces homeomorphic to Euclidean spheres, while closed balls are homeomorphic to Euclidean closed balls, and open balls are diffeomorphic to Euclidean open balls. These results improve the known ones and extend them beyond two-step distributions. The proof relies on uniform Lipschitz estimates for the distance, of independent interest.
item.dc:creator: Luca Rizzi, Giuditta Rovelli

item.title: Tunable Spatial Task Allocation with Application to Maritime Swarms
item.description: arXiv:2610.39018v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In this chapter, we explore how a team of autonomous agents can flexibly reconfigure the distribution of its members across many spatially embedded tasks using a task allocation strategy grounded in a generalization of the recently proposed Nonlinear Opinion Dynamics model. Motivated by an adaptive maritime survey application, we couple opinion dynamics directly to spatial movement and examine how the emergent macroscopic allocation is shaped by the interplay between environmental geometry, nature of social interactions, and task demands. We illustrate in simulation how social coupling in the model tunes group cohesion, producing macroscopic allocation patterns ranging from maximally dispersed states, to intermediate semi-dispersed states with a smaller number of distinct subgroups, to maximally cohesive consensus states, in distinct and interpretable parameter regimes. Furthermore, we demonstrate with illustrative examples how a team can reconfigure itself in real time under changing task demands. For allocation scenarios with distance-based task preference and matched number of agents and tasks, we relate numerically the final allocation in the group to the Hungarian optimum, illustrating close-to-optimal performance. We illustrate performance of this method under realistic communication constraints in the MOOS-IvP-Multi simulation environment with simulated autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs). Together, these examples show how a common set of local interaction rules can support a large range of interpretable macroscopic allocation states and flexible transitions between them.
item.dc:creator: Vishnudatta Thota, Tyler Paine, Anastasia Bizyaeva

item.title: Bregman projections and partition design for accelerating finite Markov chains
item.description: arXiv:2610.39239v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study Gibbs averaging of finite Markov chains with a prescribed stationary distribution $\pi$. Given a transition matrix $P$ and the Gibbs kernel $G$ induced by a state-space partition, we prove that $GPG$ is an information projection for every admissible Bregman generator $\phi$, with divergences defined using transition probabilities relative to $\pi$. A Pythagorean identity characterizes this projection and recovers the relative entropy and weighted Frobenius cases. A dual characterization identifies $GPG$ as a kernel closest to stationarity among those with the same projection chain as $P$; for relative entropy, it maximizes the entropy rate. The identities also give monotonicity under partition coarsening. For every reversible ergodic baseline $P$, Gibbs averaging cannot increase the squared weighted Frobenius distance to stationarity at any positive integer time, and the inequality is strict unless $P=GPG$. The corresponding mixing time therefore cannot increase. To choose the partition, we identify the divergence of $G$ from stationarity as the exact worst-case divergence of $GPG$ over all $\pi$-stationary baselines $P$. This objective depends only on the block masses. We give an exact algorithm for concave block costs, including those arising from relative entropy and power generators $\phi(u)=u^p$ with $1<p<2$, and a greedy approximation algorithm with a provable guarantee for $p>2$. For power generators $\phi(u)=u^p$ with $p>1$, the objective is proportional to Tsallis entropy of order $2-p$: its minimization favors imbalanced block masses when $1<p<2$ and balanced block masses when $p>2$, while all $k$-block partitions have the same objective value when $p=2$. A numerical experiment compares the resulting projected chains with a local Metropolis sampler on a multi-modal $\pi$.
item.dc:creator: Michael C. H. Choi, Youjia Wang

item.title: Linearize or Discretize First? Error Estimates under Mesh-Uniform Regularity and Exponential Stability for the KdV Equation with Boundary Dissipation
item.description: arXiv:2610.39269v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study the Korteweg-de Vries equation on a bounded interval with boundary dissipation, and its spatial semidiscretization by a weighted cubic Hermite Galerkin method. A small nonlinear wave can be approximated by a linear discrete simulation in two orders: linearize first and then discretize, or discretize first and then linearize. Both orders give the same total error, but they divide it differently between linearization and discretization. The difference of the two divisions is the ordering error. We show that it is quadratic in the size of the initial datum and carries a positive power of the mesh size, for all time. For the continuous problem, the solution map is analytic, with a power series that converges for all time in exponentially weighted trajectory norms. The linearized semigroup has Crandall-Pazy regularity with the exact index 3/2. For the weighted scheme, exponential stability, Kato smoothing, Crandall-Pazy regularity and analyticity of the solution maps hold uniformly in the mesh size. These properties give error estimates in which the error and the datum are measured in the same norm: in the energy norm, in $H_0^1$ and in $H^2$. In exponentially weighted time-integrated norms the semidiscrete solutions converge uniformly on balls, at the rate $h^{1/6}$ in $L^4(0,\infty;L^2)$ for data in $L^2$ and at the rate $h^{2/3}$ in $L^2(0,\infty;H^1)$ for data in $H_0^1$. On every interval $[t_0,\infty)$, $t_0>0$, same-norm convergence holds uniformly on balls at algebraic rates. The ordering error is of order $h^{1/6}$ times the square of the energy norm of the datum, uniformly for all $t\ge0$. For the unweighted scheme, a grid wave packet of zero group velocity destroys mesh-uniform Kato smoothing and Crandall-Pazy regularity.
item.dc:creator: Kangsheng Liu

item.title: Sharp potential and Brenier map $W_2$-stability for log-concave sources
item.description:
arXiv:2610.39272v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study stability of Brenier potentials and maps under changes of the target measure. Let $\kappa>0$, for a full support $\kappa$-strongly log-concave source $ho$, possibly with a non-smooth potential, the normalized transport potentials satisfy \[ \|u_\mu-u_

The proof controls normalized Laguerre cell barycentres by their mass derivatives and centers the potential velocity to remove unbounded source cell locations. Bounded variation interpolation then yields the sharp map exponent $1/3$ for targets in a common compact set, \[ \left\Vert T_{\mu}-T_{
u}ight\Vert _{L^{2}(ho)}\leqslant \operatorname{Const} \cdot W_{2}\left( \mu,

item.dc:creator: Yuanlong Ruan

item.title: LLM-Assisted Optimization for Simulation-Based Redesign
item.description: arXiv:2610.39275v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Engineering design frequently involves redesigning a prior solution to adapt to changes in context, such as material prices or system requirements. Redesign often leverages simulators too complex and/or computationally intensive for traditional numerical solvers, which lack engineering knowledge and context, to ensure global solution quality. Large language models (LLMs) can interpret semantic information, including engineering knowledge about the system and changes in context, to help guide search, and recent studies have shown that incorporating this knowledge into optimization can improve search performance. However, how best to combine LLMs with numerical solvers in redesign remains unclear. We develop and test an integrated LLM-optimization approach for redesign and compare three methods for leveraging LLMs (warm start, variable fixing and ReAct) and four black-box solvers (Bayesian optimization, genetic algorithms, mesh adaptive direct search and random search) on an electric vehicle battery pack cost minimization case study across four types of redesign scenarios. We find that the integrated approach can match feasible design discovery of the numerical-solver baselines with 80% fewer simulator evaluations while tripling the fraction of runs that find near-optimal solutions. We find that the best LLM-solver integration approach and the way the prior solution is leveraged depend on the structure of the design requirement change, and that the benefit of increasing LLM model size grows with the extent to which the LLM controls the search. These results show clear potential for LLMs in redesign tasks for guiding or replacing numerical solvers.
item.dc:creator: Chan-Eui Song, Jeremy J. Michalek, Christopher McComb

item.title: There Is No Free Lunch in RLVR: Every pass@1 Gain Has a pass@k Price
item.description: arXiv:2610.39295v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) makes a language model solve more problems on the first try and fewer when given many tries: it raises pass@1 while the base model overtakes it at large sampling budget k. Is this a failure of RL to add reasoning, or a transient that more training removes? We settle the question with a theorem. The reversal is a price, and we compute its exact rate. Modeling RLVR as an exponential tilt of a base policy over strategies shared across prompts, we prove that under exclusive specialization every update that raises pass@1 strictly lowers the success of some prompt; a strictly positive price on prompts (Stiemke duality) is the exact condition, and being merely the best strategy on a prompt is provably not enough. When the loss reaches the hardest prompts, it forces a pass@k crossover, and the number of crossings is at most the sign variation of the shift in per-prompt success, a totally positive bound that is tight and that recovers the known single-crossover result as its order-preserving case. The crossover is not a bug to patch: a constrained update traces the exact pass@1 versus pass@k frontier, and removing the crossover entirely costs the entire pass@1 gain. The same tilt identity yields entropy collapse and the entropy-performance law with an identifiable exponent, unifying two literatures under one mechanism. Reinforcement cannot widen the reasoning frontier; it can only move along it, at a price we make measurable by a diagnostic that reads the bound, the order-preserving test, and the price from any evaluation log. There is no free lunch, only a price.
item.dc:creator: Yinuo Liu

item.title: Information-Driven Collaborative Autonomy for Heterogeneous UAV/UGV Teams
item.description: arXiv:2610.39379v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This paper considers coordinating a heterogeneous team of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs) traversing a domain containing an unknown number of potentially hazardous targets. The UAVs provide aerial sensing using onboard optical cameras, adapting their trajectories to ground routes and target information. We formulate the aerial search problem using ergodic control, which distributes sensing effort according to a spatial information density to balance exploration and target localization. The formulation incorporates dynamic camera field-of-view footprints and pose-dependent probabilistic detection models. Angles-only measurements are processed through Bayesian inference and marginalization over data-association hypotheses to obtain a Poisson multi-Bernoulli (PMB) approximation of the target posterior, representing both detected and undetected targets. This belief directs aerial sensing toward unexplored regions along the ground routes and viewpoints that improve target localization. Ground planning combines chance-constrained target avoidance, enforced through confidence sets, with a void-probability objective that favors routes unlikely to contain threats. We solve each team's optimization problem in a fully decentralized manner using a nested SCvx*--C-ADMM scheme, with outer sequential convex programming iterations and inner distributed consensus optimization, accounting for nonlinearities, nonseparable objectives, and continuous-time inter-agent separation constraints. A closed-loop scheme updates both fleets' trajectories as information becomes available and permits ground motion when the remaining route risk falls below a prescribed threshold. Numerical case studies examine sensing geometry and target uncertainty, compare decentralized and centralized solvers, and demonstrate full closed-loop collaboration between multiple UAVs and UGVs.
item.dc:creator: Joshua Yuriv Pilipovsky

item.title: Safe Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning: Zero Constraint Violation and Primal-Averaging Convergence
item.description: arXiv:2610.39409v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Many applications of multi-objective reinforcement learning (MORL) require policies that balance conflicting objectives while satisfying safety constraints. We study safe MORL with zero constraint violation throughout learning, covering both cumulative and stepwise constraints. A key challenge is to explore sufficiently under unknown dynamics and constraint costs without violating the constraints. For a given preference over objectives, we develop an algorithm to learn a safe Pareto optimal policy by combining optimistic reward estimates with pessimistic cost bounds. With high probability, every policy executed over $T$ episodes incurs zero constraint violation. The algorithm returns a safe Markov policy induced by the averaged occupancy measure and achieves an $\widetilde{O}(1/\sqrt{T})$ suboptimality gap under smooth Tchebycheff scalarization. We further develop a preference-free algorithm that first explores safely without a prespecified preference and then computes a safe policy for any given preference without further interaction. Over $T$ exploration episodes and $K$ planning iterations, it retains the same safety guarantee and achieves an $\widetilde{O}(1/\sqrt{T}+1/\sqrt{K})$ suboptimality gap. Both algorithms require knowledge of a policy that strictly satisfies the constraints and its costs. We then relax these requirements, incurring at most constant cumulative violation. To our knowledge, we provide the first sample-efficient MORL algorithms that guarantee safety for every executed policy.
item.dc:creator: Chenxi Li, Yao Shu, Siyang Gao, Shuang Qiu, Guangxin Jiang

item.title: Dobb: Shard-Local Preconditioning in Block-Diagonal Eigenbases
item.description: arXiv:2610.39412v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Training language models whose parameters and optimizer state exceed a single node's memory requires sharding these tensors across devices. Under tensor parallelism (TP) or fully sharded data parallelism (FSDP), matrix-aware optimizers such as Muon introduce communication to perform global matrix operations across shards. We propose Dobb (Distributed Optimizer with Block-diagonal Eigenbases), a matrix-aware optimizer designed to compute updates locally within parameter shards. Dobb approximates the input-activation second moment with diagonal blocks and tracks a complete basis within each block. It projects momentum into these bases, applies sign normalization to the coefficients, and reconstructs the update. When each block lies within one shard under TP or FSDP, Dobb applies its matrix update locally, requiring no communication beyond data-parallel synchronization of the activation second moments. We benchmark Dobb against Dion, a distributed matrix-aware optimizer designed to retain the benefits of orthonormalized updates while reducing communication. On GPT-2 XL (1.56B parameters), Dobb with 16 blocks reaches a validation loss of 2.476, compared with 2.511 for Dion at rank fraction 1/16. Under FSDP on 32 H100 GPUs, Dobb reduces the amortized optimizer-call time from 124.1 ms for Dion to 9.2 ms.
item.dc:creator: Shi-Yuk Fong, Shuhua Yu, Jiawei Zhang

item.title: Optimality of the BCC lattice among 3D lattice quantizers
item.description: arXiv:2610.39705v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study the problem of the best approximation (w.r.t. the optimal transport metric $W_p$, $p \in [1,\infty)$) of the three-dimensional Lebesgue measure on a domain of volume 1 by a discrete probability measure supported on a Bravais lattice. This problem is known as the quantization problem and it arises in numerical integration, electrical engineering, discrete geometry and materials science. As the lattice size tends to zero and the cardinality of the support of the discrete measure tends to infinity, this reduces to the following geometric optimization problem: Amongst three-dimensional Bravais lattices with determinant $1$, which lattice minimises the $p$-th moment of the lattice Voronoi cell? Barnes and Sloane (1983) proved that the BCC lattice is optimal for the case $p=2$, which is known as the vector quantization problem in the signal compression literature. Bambah (1954) proved that the BCC lattice is optimal for the limiting case $p=\infty$, which is the sphere covering problem. Based on these results, Graf and Luschgy (2000) conjectured that the BCC lattice is optimal for all $p \in [1,\infty)$. Three dimensions is the critical dimension in the sense that in two dimensions the optimal lattice is independent of $p$, whereas in four dimensions it varies with $p$. In this paper we give support in favour of Graf and Luschgy's conjecture by proving that the BCC lattice is a local minimiser for all $p \in [1,\infty)$ and a global minimiser for $p$ near 2. While the conjecture asserts that the global minimiser is independent of $p$, we prove a bifurcation theorem which shows that the set of critical points depends on $p$ and that $p=2$ is a distinguished case. Our proofs combine results from discrete geometry by Barnes and Sloane (1983) and Conway and Sloane (1992) with optimal transport theory, the calculus of variations, bifurcation theory, and some delicate positivity estimates.
item.dc:creator: David P. Bourne, Filippo Cagnetti, Steven M. Roper

item.title: Implicit Bias of (Stochastic) Gradient Descent on Deep Linear Diagonal Networks
item.description: arXiv:2610.39717v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Modern machine learning models are often overparameterized, i.e., have more parameters than training data. This typically implies that the loss function admits multiple minimizers so that training methods (and their hyperparameter choices) have significant influence on the computed solution. We study this so-called implicit bias phenomenon in the context of training deep linear diagonal networks. Previous work has shown that the gradient flow for learning such networks converges to (almost) sparse solutions when initialized small. For an arbitrary number of layers, we extend this analysis to the practically more realistic (stochastic) gradient descent iterations. Our approach identifies (stochastic) gradient descent as a perturbed (stochastic) mirror gradient descent. This allows us to establish convergence and characterize the limiting solution, relating it to weighted $\ell_1$-minimization. Moreover, we provide sufficient conditions on the step sizes and quantify the influence of the step sizes on the implicit bias.
item.dc:creator: Wiebke Bartolomaeus, Holger Rauhut

item.title: When to spend privacy: optimal allocation in private learning
item.description: arXiv:2610.39954v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Privacy accounting bounds the cumulative privacy cost of Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent but does not determine how to allocate a fixed budget across iterations. We formulate the complete Gaussian noise-variance schedule as an open-loop control under a composed zero-Concentrated Differential Privacy constraint, explicitly accounting for schedule selection. For expected quadratic terminal tracking, we prove that every local minimizer exhausts the certified budget, yielding an exact-budget simplex formulation. We introduce Privacy-Budget Adjoint Mirror Descent (PB-AMD), combining pathwise adjoint gradients with entropic updates that preserve positivity, charge floors, and the prescribed budget. Under regularity and coercivity assumptions, we establish existence and budget stability of optimal schedules, design-to-training utility stability, and deterministic, stochastic, and sample-average stationarity guarantees. A linear-quadratic reduction yields an explicit square-root allocation law. Experiments demonstrate tracking improvements over several allocation rules and predictive improvements over uniform allocation in a learning-rate restart setting, where learning-rate allocation performs similarly. Comparisons at a common stationarity tolerance show lower schedule-optimization times than projected gradient descent on the tested problems. The framework connects certified privacy accounting with optimization through nonlinear training dynamics.
item.dc:creator: Umberto Biccari, Yongcun Song

item.title: Data-driven Regularization for Inverse Problems
item.description: arXiv:2610.40048v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In many applications, we are interested in studying an object of interest $x$. However, its properties are often not directly measurable. Instead, we only observe $y = F(x)$, where the (known) function $F$ is referred to as the forward mapping. To infer about $x$ from the observation $y$, we seek an (approximate) inverse mapping $x \approx F^{-1}(y)$. This process is known as solving the inverse problem. In practice, the inverse mapping $F^{-1}$ may be ill-defined or discontinuous, which forces us to choose a certain solution from many possible ones based on prior assumptions on $x$. Such assumptions about $x$ are typically incorporated into the inversion process through regularization. Therefore, the first part of this course focuses on the classical regularization theory of inverse problems. In the second part, we transition to algorithmic approaches for solving inverse problems. The foundation for this lies in the variational formulation of inverse problems, where reconstructions are obtained by minimizing specific functionals. Here, we will explore key optimization principles, discuss their practical implementation, and examine how they contribute to robust reconstructions. Today, classical methods are often modified to incorporate data-driven machine learning techniques, which improve the empirical performance. However, this often comes at the cost of explainability or convergence guarantees. Such properties are critical, for example, in medical applications, where one wants to be confident that reconstructed abnormalities are of physical nature and not phantoms resulting from the method. For these reasons, we discuss a number of machine learning methods for inverse problems, such as unrolling techniques, learned regularizers and plug-and-play methods, and explore their performance guarantees.
item.dc:creator: Oleh Melnyk, Sebastian Neumayer

item.title: Readiness-Constrained Pre-Islanding Dispatch for Military Microgrids
item.description: arXiv:2610.40078v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Military installation energy readiness depends on having sufficient resources to sustain mission-critical loads throughout a prolonged utility outage. This paper develops a method to help operators manage energy resources during normal grid-connected operation while preserving islanded readiness. A robust viability kernel identifies combinations of battery energy, fuel, and load-shifting capability sufficient to sustain critical load under uncertain demand and photovoltaic generation. A probability bound translates stochastic generator start failures and recovery into a deterministic generator count selected to meet a specified availability requirement at islanding. Case studies for a fourteen-day islanding requirement at 0.999 islanding-entry availability show that advance warning of an outage can be used to prepare resources to meet a higher readiness requirement before islanding begins. The case studies further demonstrate that economic-only operation and the evaluated fixed battery reserve policy can fail to sustain critical load for the required duration, whereas enforcing the resource-dependent requirement preserves readiness at a modest increase in modeled grid-connected operating cost. These results demonstrate how active resource management can preserve long-duration energy readiness. The framework also helps commanders understand how readiness changes with operating conditions, even when the available resources remain the same.
item.dc:creator: Aidan Looney, Annie Weathers, Nicholas Judson

item.title: A lifted entropy splitting lemma and applications
item.description: arXiv:2610.40145v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We give a matrix lifting of the entropy-splitting theorem of Csisz\'ar, K\"orner, Lov\'asz, Marton, and Simonyi, and show several applications. We use it to prove the Cartesian-product inequality conjectured by Sinjorgo and Sotirov for the generalized Lov\'asz theta number, and we also answer the saturation and convexification questions of Carli Silva, Coutinho, Oliveira, and Tun\c{c}el on the same theme. For the strong Hoffman bound, we answer a question of Wocjan, Elphick, and Darbari concerning orthogonal rank, and show that optimization over matrix weights gives exactly the ceiling of the theta number of the complement. Finally, we extend the lifting to diagonally invariant cones of positive semidefinite matrices, giving a proof of a conjecture by Kuryatnikova, Sotirov, and Vera, and giving a short proof, for all graphs, of a theta-based weakening of Fajtlowicz's graph-energy conjecture.
item.dc:creator: Gabriel Coutinho, Luis Higino

item.title: Finite-Sample LTI System Identification from a Misspecified Finite Model Set
item.description: arXiv:2610.40387v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We consider the problem of finite-sample identification of an unknown LTI system from a finite hypothesis class. In contrast to existing results that assume the hypothesis class contains the true system, we consider the misspecified setting, where the true system does not belong to the hypothesis class. We first characterize the resulting estimation target and its dependence on the data-generation scheme. We then establish a finite-sample lower bound on the failure probability that any identification algorithm must incur. Finally, we analyze the robustness of an existing exponential weighting-based identification algorithm to the misspecification and derive a finite-sample upper bound on its failure probability. Our results illustrate when using a misspecified finite hypothesis class can provide an advantage over identification without prior knowledge of the candidate systems.
item.dc:creator: Nicolas Chatzikiriakos, Andrea Iannelli

item.title: First-Order Bilevel Optimization for Non-truthful Auction Design
item.description: arXiv:2610.40403v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Automated mechanism design has enabled the learning of complex auction mechanisms using neural networks. However, designing non-truthful auctions remains challenging because bidders' equilibrium strategies depend on the auction mechanism and thus evolve as the mechanism is optimized. In this work, we formulate auction design as a Stackelberg game with multiple strategic followers and develop a fully first-order algorithm for revenue optimization in non-truthful auctions. We establish non-asymptotic guarantees for hypergradient approximation and show that, under standard smoothness and strong-monotonicity assumptions, our method reaches an $O(\epsilon)$-stationary point using $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\epsilon^{-2})$ first-order oracle calls. Experiments on symmetric and asymmetric single-item auctions, as well as multi-item auctions, show that our method converges faster than second- and zeroth-order baselines and scales better as the number of bidders increases. Our method also discovers auctions that achieve revenue close to truthful baselines. These results provide a scalable framework for automated mechanism design beyond truthful auctions.
item.dc:creator: Shing-Hei Ho, April Niu, Ellen Vitercik, Kai Wang

item.title: Aerodynamic Shape Optimization of unsteady flapping wings
item.description: arXiv:2610.40426v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This study introduces a new approach for building surrogate models, in the form of Reduced Order Models (ROMs), for PDE-constrained optimization. A physics-constrained data-driven framework is developed to transform large-scale non-linear optimization problems into ROM-constrained optimization problems. Unlike conventional methods, which suffer from instability of the forward sensitivity function, the proposed approach projects optimization problems to system dynamics optimization problems in Hilbert space to increase stability, diminish memory requirements, and lower computational cost. The present approach is applied to shape optimization of a 2D flapping wing section at $Re=2,400$, where the non-linear interaction of the wing with fluid includes chaotic flow structures. It is shown that the proposed approach can significantly enhance the time-averaged thrust force and propulsive efficiency by 37\% and 40\%, respectively. We also tested this approach for a 3D flapping wing and the results reveal the potential of the proposed approach for more complex optimal designs in the aerospace industry.
item.dc:creator: Hamid R. Karbasian, Brian C. Vermeire

item.title: Adaptive search with path-constrained mobile sensors using multi-arm bandits
item.description: arXiv:2610.40431v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study a constrained sequential decision problem for detecting regions of interest from noisy online measurements collected by a team of energy-constrained mobile sensors. The sensor motion is restricted to a precomputed set of feasible paths that satisfy mobility constraints, limited available energy by requiring return to charging stations, and avoidance of known obstacles. We cast the resulting active path selection as a multi-armed bandit problem and propose an iterative search algorithm that adaptively assigns paths using confidence bounds computed from the collected data. We also propose a graph-based method to construct low-cardinality path covers under the team's constraints. We establish finite-time and anytime probabilistic correctness guarantees for the proposed algorithm, derive non-asymptotic upper bounds on the times required to detect all regions of interest and to label all nodes, and show that these bounds match algorithm-independent lower bounds up to constant factors for a broad class of problem instances. Using numerical simulations, we illustrate the behavior of the proposed approach and the effect of path redundancy and team size on search performance.
item.dc:creator: Abraham P. Vinod, Parth K. Thaker, Gautam Dasarathy, Stefano Di Cairano

item.title: Random Matching Between Distinct Distributions in Two Dimensions
item.description: arXiv:2610.40509v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Given two independent $n$-point samples drawn from possibly distinct probability distributions on a compact 2-dimensional surface, we minimize the total squared distance over all perfect bipartite matchings. Under regularity assumptions, the expected matching cost minus $n$ times the squared 2-Wasserstein distance between the sampling distributions grows logarithmically with $n$. We determine this difference up to an additive $o(1)$ error, including the dependence of the logarithmic coefficient and constant term on geometry and sampling distributions, and establish the existence of a universal constant shared by these formulas. Our analysis expresses the expected matching cost in terms of the cost of transporting a heat-smoothed sample back to its original points. The reductions giving this relation hold in every dimension and for general costs under suitable assumptions, with consequences beyond the setting studied here. In two dimensions, the relation is exact up to an additive $o(1)$ error, so determining the matching cost amounts to evaluating the smoothing cost with the same accuracy. We obtain this evaluation by subdividing the domain and exploiting cancellations between the sample and its own smoothing.
item.dc:creator: Yunzong Xu

item.title: The Number of Tropical Order Types and Coherent Matching Fields
item.description: arXiv:2610.40622v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We investigate counting problems for discrete (geometric) structures in tropical settings, motivated by the comparison of the expressivity of linear programs and mean-payoff games. First, we give an upper bound on the number of coherent matching fields of type $(n,r)$ and a lower bound on the number of combinatorial types of $n$-hyperplane sequences in the max-plus tropical space of dimension $r-1$. These structures are closely related, and our bounds establish that as $n \to \infty$, for every fixed $r$ their number equals $n^{(r-1)^2n+o(n)}$. This in turn implies that the number of regular triangulations of the products of simplices $\Delta^{n-1}\times\Delta^{r-1}$ is also $n^{(r-1)^2n+o(n)}$, thereby answering a question of Santos. Second, we obtain that the number of labeled order types over the reals and over the signed tropical numbers coincide at first order, establishing a comparison of the expressivity of mean-payoff games and linear programs as measured by labeled order types. Last, the subclass of mean-payoff games known as parity games arise from linear programs by a ``double tropicalization.'' We show that the number of labeled order types obtained after this double tropicalization collapses.
item.dc:creator: Xavier Allamigeon, Yiyuan Chen, St\'ephane Gaubert, Xavier Goaoc

item.title: Data-driven Wasserstein distributionally robust generalized Nash equilibrium problems with heterogeneous uncertainty
item.description: arXiv:2312.03573v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study stochastic generalized Nash equilibrium (GNE) problems with heterogeneous, stochastic uncertainty in the cost functions. To address the distributional uncertainty, we let each agent construct an individual Wasserstein ambiguity set around an empirical distribution obtained from private data. We establish finite-sample robustness guarantees for any distributionally robust (DR) GNE. Focusing on variational equilibria, we derive a DR variational inequality (VI) reformulation and establish asymptotic consistency with the nominal stochastic game. Under mild conditions, we derive an exact finite-dimensional generalized Nash equilibrium reformulation. We then quantify how heterogeneous worst-case distributions affect monotonicity, and derive conditions for uniqueness and equilibrium sensitivity. To compute a variational DR GNE, we propose an inexact projected method and establish convergence under vanishing oracle errors, an asymptotic error bound under bounded oracle errors, and linear convergence under exact oracle evaluations.
item.dc:creator: Georgios Pantazis, Barbara Franci, Sergio Grammatico

item.title: A particle system approach towards the global well-posedness of master equations for potential mean field games of control
item.description: arXiv:2412.11742v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper studies the $N$-particle systems as well as the HJB/master equations for a class of generalized mean field control (MFC) problems and the corresponding potential mean field games of control (MFGC). A local in time classical solution for the HJB equation is generated via a probabilistic approach based on the mean field maximum principle. Given an extension of the so called displacement convexity condition, we obtain the uniform estimates on the HJB equation for the $N$-particle system. Such estimates imply the displacement convexity/semi-concavity and thus the prior estimates on the solution to the HJB equation for generalized MFC problems. The global well-posedness of HJB/master equation for generalized MFC/potential MFGC is then proved thanks to the local well-posedness and the prior estimates. In view of the nature of the displacement convexity condition, such well-posedness is also true for the degenerated case. Our analysis on the $N$-particle system also induces an Lipschitz approximator to the optimal feedback function in generalized MFC/potential MFGC where an algebraic convergence rate is obtained. Furthermore, an alternative approximate Nash equilibrium is proposed based on the $N$-particle system, where the approximation error is quantified thanks to the aforementioned uniform estimates.
item.dc:creator: Huafu Liao, Chenchen Mou

item.title: A Linear Parameter-Varying Framework for the Analysis of Time-Varying Optimization Algorithms
item.description: arXiv:2501.07461v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this paper we propose a framework to analyze iterative first-order optimization algorithms for time-varying convex optimization. We assume that the temporal variability is caused by a time-varying parameter entering the objective, which can be measured at the time of decision but whose future values are unknown. We consider the case of strongly convex objective functions with Lipschitz continuous gradients under a convex constraint set. We model the algorithms as discrete-time linear parameter varying (LPV) systems in feedback with monotone operators such as the time-varying gradient. We leverage the approach of analyzing algorithms as uncertain control interconnections with integral quadratic constraints (IQCs) and generalize that framework to the time-varying case. We propose novel IQCs that are capable of capturing the behavior of time-varying nonlinearities and leverage techniques from the LPV literature to establish novel bounds on the tracking error. Quantitative bounds can be computed by solving a semi-definite program and can be interpreted as an input-to-state stability result with respect to a disturbance signal which increases with the temporal variability of the problem. As a departure from results in this research area, our bounds introduce a dependence on different additional measures of temporal variations, such as the function value and gradient rate of change. We exemplify our main results with numerical experiments that showcase how our analysis framework is able to capture convergence rates of different first-order algorithms for time-varying optimization through the choice of IQC and rate bounds.
item.dc:creator: Fabian Jakob, Andrea Iannelli

item.title: A Practical GPU-Enhanced Matrix-Free Primal-Dual Method for Large-Scale Conic Programs
item.description: arXiv:2505.00311v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this paper, we introduce a practical GPU-enhanced matrix-free first-order method for solving large-scale conic programming problems, which we refer to as PDCS, standing for the Primal-Dual Conic Programming Solver. Problems that it solves include linear programs, second-order cone programs, convex quadratic programs, and exponential cone programs. The method avoids matrix factorizations and uses sparse matrix-vector multiplication as its core operation, which is memory-efficient and well suited for GPU acceleration. It builds on a variant of the primal-dual hybrid gradient method (PDHG) called reflected restarted Halpern PDHG with averaging, which we prove converges on general conic programs, and further incorporates several practical enhancements. Its GPU implementation, cuPDCS, uses customized computational schemes that assign cones of different types and sizes to different levels of the GPU architecture. Numerical experiments demonstrate that cuPDCS is generally more efficient than state-of-the-art commercial solvers and other first-order methods on large-scale conic program applications, including Fisher market equilibrium problems, Lasso regression, and multi-period portfolio optimization. cuPDCS also exhibits better scalability, efficiency, and robustness compared to other first-order methods on the conic program benchmark dataset CBLIB. These advantages are more pronounced in large-scale settings.
item.dc:creator: Zhenwei Lin, Zikai Xiong, Dongdong Ge, Yinyu Ye

item.title: A Path Planning Model for Intercepting a Moving Target with Finite Obstacle Avoidance
item.description: arXiv:2507.01447v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper investigates the problem of computing a two-dimensional curvature-constrained shortest path for an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) to intercept a moving target, with both the UAV (pursuer) and the target traveling at constant speeds. We formulate an optimal control problem that integrates two critical objectives: avoiding static obstacles and successfully intercepting the target. The formulation integrates curvature constraints, geometric obstacle-avoidance conditions, and time-consistent interception constraints within a constrained optimal control framework. A geometric framework is developed, along with necessary conditions for path optimality under the imposed constraints. The problem is initially examined in the presence of a single obstacle and later extended to scenarios involving a finite number of obstacles. Numerical experiments are carried out to evaluate the performance and efficiency of the proposed model using illustrative examples. Finally, we present a realistic case study using actual geographic data, including obstacle placement, target trajectory, and heading angles, to demonstrate the practical applicability and effectiveness of the proposed method in real-world scenarios.
item.dc:creator: Masuda Akter, Mohammed Mustafa Rizvi

item.title: Second-order sequential optimality conditions for nonlinear semidefinite optimization problems
item.description: arXiv:2507.21495v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Sequential optimality conditions play an important role in constrained optimization since they provide necessary conditions without requiring constraint qualifications (CQs). This paper introduces a second-order extension of the Approximate Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (AKKT) conditions, referred to as AKKT2, for nonlinear semidefinite optimization problems (NSDP). In particular, we provide a formal definition of AKKT2, as well as its stronger variant, called Complementary AKKT2 (CAKKT2), and prove that these conditions are necessary for local minima without any assumption. Moreover, under Robinson's CQ and the weak constant rank property, we show that AKKT2 implies the so-called weak second-order necessary condition. Finally, we propose a penalty method and show that, under an assumption related to the Lojasiewicz inequality, its accumulation points satisfy the AKKT2 and CAKKT2 conditions.
item.dc:creator: Huimin Li, Yuya Yamakawa, Ellen H. Fukuda

item.title: On the controllability of the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation on multi-dimensional cylindrical domains
item.description: arXiv:2508.00812v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this article, we investigate null controllability of the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky (KS) equation on a cylindrical domain $\Omega=\Omega_x\times \Omega_y$ in $\mathbb R^N$, where $\Omega_x=(0,a),$ $a>0$ and $\Omega_y$ is a smooth domain in $\mathbb R^{N-1}$. We first study the controllability of this system by a control acting on $\{0\}\times \omega$, $\omega\subset \Omega_y$, through the boundary term associated with the Laplacian component. The null controllability of the linearized system is proved using a combination of two techniques: the method of moments and Lebeau-Robbiano strategy. We provide a necessary and sufficient condition for the null controllability of this system along with an explicit control cost estimate. Furthermore, we show that there exists minimal time $T_0(x_0)>0$ such that the system is null controllable for all time $T > T_0(x_0)$ by means of an interior control exerted on $\gamma = \{x_0\} \times \omega \subset \Omega$, where $x_0/a\in (0,1)\setminus \mathbb{Q}$ and it is not controllable if $T<T_0(x_0).$ If we assume $x_0/a$ is an algebraic real number of order $d > 1$, then we prove the controllability for any time $T>0.$ Finally, for the case of $N=2 \text{ or } 3$, we show the local null controllability of the main nonlinear system by employing the source term method followed by the Banach fixed point theorem.
item.dc:creator: V\'ictor Hern\'andez-Santamar\'ia, Subrata Majumdar

item.title: Clapping: Removing Per-sample Storage for Pipeline Parallel Distributed Optimization with Communication Compression
item.description: arXiv:2509.19029v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Pipeline-parallel distributed optimization is essential for large-scale machine learning but is challenged by significant communication overhead from transmitting high-dimensional activations and gradients between workers. Existing approaches often depend on impractical unbiased gradient assumptions or incur sample-size memory overhead. This paper introduces Clapping, a Communication compression algorithm with LAzy samPling for Pipeline-parallel learnING. Clapping adopts a lazy sampling strategy that reuses data samples across steps, breaking sample-wise memory barrier and supporting convergence in few-epoch or online regimes. Clapping comprises two variants including Clapping-FC and Clapping-FU, both of which achieve convergence without unbiased assumption for compressed gradient, effectively addressing compression error propagation in multi-worker settings. Numerical experiments validate the performance of Clapping across different tasks.
item.dc:creator: Boao Kong, Xu Huang, Yuqi Xu, Yixuan Liang, Bin Wang, Kun Yuan

item.title: A Compressive Sensing Inspired Monte-Carlo Method for Combinatorial Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2510.24755v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this paper, we present a Monte-Carlo Compressive Optimization algorithm, a new method for black-box combinatorial optimization, which only assumes that the objective is compressible. The method relies on random queries to the objective function in order to estimate generalized moments. Next, a greedy algorithm from compressive sensing is repurposed to find the global optimum when not overfitting to the samples. We provide numerical results giving evidence that our method is competitive by comparing it with digital annealing. Moreover, we give theoretical justification for the success of the algorithm and analyze its properties. The practicality of our algorithm is enhanced by the ability to tune the heuristic parameters to the available computational resources. An end-to-end open-source implementation is available to use our method.
item.dc:creator: Baptiste Chevalier, Shimpei Yamaguchi, Wojciech Roga, Masahiro Takeoka

item.title: Stochastic Optimal Control Problems for the Cost-Optimal Management of a Standalone Microgrid
item.description: arXiv:2511.00167v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this paper, we consider a domestic standalone microgrid equipped with local renewable energy generation such as photovoltaic panels, consumption units, and battery storage to balance supply and demand and investigate the stochastic optimal control problem for its cost-optimal management. As a special feature, the manager does not have access to the power grid but has a local generator, making it possible to produce energy using fuel when needed. Such systems are very important for rural electrification, particularly in developing countries. However, these systems are very complex to control due to uncertainties in the weather and environmental conditions, which affect the energy generation and the energy demand. In addition, we assume that the battery and the fuel tank have limited capacities and that the fuel tank can only be filled once at the beginning of the planning period. This leads us to the so-called finite fuel problem. In addition, we allow the energy demand to not always be satisfied, and we impose penalties on unsatisfied demand, the so-called discomfort cost. The main goal is to minimize the expected aggregated cost of generating power using the generator and operating the system. This leads to a mathematical optimization problem. The problem is formulated as a discrete-time stochastic control problem and solved numerically using methods from the theory of Markov decision processes.
item.dc:creator: Paul Honore Takam, Nathalie Fruiba

item.title: Complete Characterizations of Well-Posedness in Parametric Composite Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2512.14124v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper characterizes the well-posedness of Karush-Kuhn-Tucker system for perturbed composite optimization. Using the parabolic regularity, we introduce a novel second-order variational function, shown to be the pivotal object governing second-order behavior. This foundational result yields the strong second-order sufficient condition introduced here for the general class of composite optimization problems to naturally extend the classical second-order sufficient condition in nonlinear programming. Then we obtain several equivalent characterizations of the second-order qualification condition (SOQC) and highlight its relationship with the constraint nondegeneracy condition under the $\mathcal{C}^{2}$-cone reducibility assumption. These insights lead us to multiple equivalent conditions for the major Lipschitz-like/Aubin property of KKT systems, including SOQC combined with the new second-order subdifferential condition and SOQC combined with tilt stability of local minimizers. Under the $\mathcal{C}^{2}$-cone reducibility, we settle the long-standing question by proving the equivalence between the Aubin property of KKT systems around local minimizers and the classical notion of strong regularity. Finally, we demonstrate that the Lipschitz-like property is equivalent to the nonsingularity of the generalized Jacobian associated with the KKT system under a certain verifiable assumption. These results provide a unified and rigorous framework for analyzing stability and sensitivity of solutions to composite optimization problems, as well as for the design and justification of numerical algorithms.
item.dc:creator: Boris S. Mordukhovich, Peipei Tang, Chengjing Wang

item.title: Discrete-Time Mean Field Type Games: Probabilistic Setup
item.description: arXiv:2512.24313v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We introduce a general probabilistic framework for discrete-time, infinite-horizon discounted Mean Field Type Games (MFTGs) with both global common noise and team-specific common noises. In our model, agents are allowed to use randomized actions, both at the individual level and at the team level. We formalize the concept of Mean Field Markov Games (MFMGs) and establish a connection between closed-loop policies in MFTGs and Markov policies in MFMGs through different layers of randomization. By leveraging recent results on infinite-horizon discounted games with infinite compact state-action spaces, we prove the existence of a stationary Nash-equilibrium profile of closed-loop policies for the original MFTG when the state spaces and the action spaces are compact Polish spaces. We also present an example satisfying our assumptions.
item.dc:creator: Gr\'egoire Lambrecht, Mathieu Lauri\`ere

item.title: Penalty-Based Smoothing and Accelerated Inertial Dynamics for Convex Supremum Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2601.15208v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study dual-penalty smoothing for convex functions with a finite-dimensional supremum representation. The regularization yields a differentiable surrogate with controlled approximation error, a single-valued dual maximizer, and explicit gradient formulas. We then study an accelerated inertial dynamic with vanishing damping driven by a time-dependent regularized function whose parameter decreases to zero. The global well-posedness of this system is not an immediate consequence of standard ODE theory, since the gradient of the regularized objective is in general only locally Lipschitz and its local Lipschitz modulus may deteriorate as the smoothing parameter vanishes. We therefore establish existence and uniqueness of global trajectories through a local well-posedness analysis and a continuation argument. Then, assuming that the original problem has a minimizer and under mild integrability conditions on the regularization schedule, we establish an accelerated $\mathcal{O}(t^{-2})$ decay estimate for the regularized and original objective values and, in the regime $\alpha>3$, a sharper $o(t^{-2})$ decay together with weak convergence of trajectories to a minimizer of the original nonsmooth problem via an Opial-type argument. Applications to multiobjective optimization (through Chebyshev/max scalarization) and to distributionally robust optimization (via entropic regularization over ambiguity sets) illustrate the scope of the framework.
item.dc:creator: Samir Adly, Juan Jos\'e Maul\'en, Emilio Vilches

item.title: Heterogeneous Distributed Zeroth-Order Nonconvex Optimization with Communication Compression
item.description: arXiv:2602.08659v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Distributed zeroth-order optimization is increasingly applied in heterogeneous scenarios where agents possess distinct data distributions and objectives. This heterogeneity poses fundamental challenges for convergence analysis, as existing convergence analyses rely on relatively strong assumptions to ensure theoretical guarantees. Specifically, at least one of the following three assumptions is usually required: (i) data homogeneity across agents, (ii) $\mathcal{O}(pn)$ function evaluations per iteration with $p$ denoting the dimension and $n$ the number of agents, or (iii) the Polyak--{\L}ojasiewicz (P--L) or strong convexity condition with a known corresponding constant. To overcome these limitations, we propose a Heterogeneous Distributed Zeroth-Order Compressed (HEDZOC) algorithm, which is based on a two-point zeroth-order gradient estimator and a general class of compressors. Without assuming data homogeneity, we develop the analysis covering three settings: general nonconvex functions, functions satisfying the P--L condition without knowing the P--L constant, and those with a known constant. To the best of our knowledge, the proposed HEDZOC algorithm is the first distributed zeroth-order method that establishes convergence without relying on the above three assumptions. Moreover, it achieves linear speedup convergence rate, which is comparable to state-of-the-art results attainable under data homogeneity and exact communication assumptions. Finally, experiments on heterogeneous adversarial example generation validate the theoretical results.
item.dc:creator: Haonan Wang, Xinlei Yi, Yiguang Hong, Minghui Liwang

item.title: A Pricing-for-Integrality Primal Heuristic for Branch-and-Price: An Application to the Electric Vehicle Routing Problem with Time Windows and Charging Time Slots
item.description: arXiv:2602.08673v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Branch-price-and-cut is the state-of-the-art exact method for solving many types of vehicle routing problems, and it is particularly effective for vehicle routing problems with time windows. A well-known challenge in branch-price-and-cut is that the generation of columns is guided by information from the linear relaxation of the master problem, with no guarantee that they will be useful from an integer perspective. As a consequence, high-quality primal solutions are often found only after significant cutting and branching, or the use of primal heuristics. In this work, based on the ideas of pricing-for-integrality, we propose a primal heuristic for branch-and-price and evaluate it on the electric vehicle routing problem with time windows extended with charging time slots. The heuristic first uses a destroy-and-repair phase to enrich the column pool and then applies a restricted master heuristic to obtain a primal solution. In the destroy-and-repair phase, route generation is guided by scaled dual values and heuristic feedback based on previously generated routes, with the aim of producing routes likely to contribute to high-quality integer solutions. Computational tests on the electric vehicle routing problem with time windows extended with charging time slots show that the proposed heuristic reduces the average optimality gap in the root node by around 60% compared to a restricted master heuristic and by around 25% - 30% compared to the implemented benchmark diving heuristic.
item.dc:creator: Lukas Eveborn, Elina R\"onnberg

item.title: Continuous-Time Heterogeneous Agent Models with Recursive Utility and Preference for Late Resolution
item.description: arXiv:2603.07782v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We consider continuous-time heterogeneous agent models with recursive utility (Epstein-Zin utility) cast as mean field games, in which agents prefer late resolution of uncertainty. The model leads to a system coupling a pair of Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equations with state constraints and Fokker-Planck-Kolmogorov equations. We investigate the existence of solutions to the mean field game system and discuss some important qualitative features of the model.
item.dc:creator: Yves Achdou, Qing Tang

item.title: State-constrained optimal control of the continuity equation and infinite-dimensional viscosity solutions
item.description: arXiv:2604.01768v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study a finite horizon optimal control problem for the continuity equation under a weighted integral state constraint on the mass outside a fixed set. The model is cast in a Hilbert framework for densities. On a suitable invariant compact subset, we prove that the value function is Lipschitz continuous and satisfies, by dynamic programming, the associated infinite dimensional constrained Hamilton Jacobi Bellman equation in viscosity sense (subsolution in the interior, supersolution up to the boundary). We finally prove a comparison principle and uniqueness in the Lipschitz class.
item.dc:creator: Fabio Bagagiolo, Ivan Roman\`o

item.title: On-Trip Matching and Pricing for Shared Rides
item.description: arXiv:2604.17552v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Shared rides, which match compatible riders in one vehicle, have the potential to increase vehicle utilization and reduce congestion and emissions. However, this service has seen limited success outside dense urban areas due to insufficient matching opportunities. The dominant model in the literature, which we refer to as the pre-trip model, matches riders before dispatch using non-bipartite matching, and dispatches unmatched riders solo. In practice, augmenting this pre-trip matching mechanism with an on-trip matching phase, where riders initially dispatched solo can still match with later arrivals, can expand matching opportunities. Yet the addition of the on-trip phase complicates the dynamic matching problem, as riders' matching opportunities evolve as they travel: both the set of compatible riders and the value of matches can diminish as a rider progresses towards her destination. To address this challenge, we formulate a Markov decision process that tracks riders' evolving states and weighs immediate matches against future matching opportunities. Within this framework, we incorporate pricing decisions to maximize long-run average profit, where we develop a fluid relaxation for static pricing and use value function approximation for dynamic (state-dependent) pricing. Experiments using Chicago ridesharing data show that pre-trip matching performs well with concentrated demand, whereas on-trip matching is particularly beneficial in the sparse outskirts where operating shared rides is especially challenging. Across both static and dynamic pricing settings, adding on-trip matching increases platform profit and match rates while lowering average quoted prices, showing the value of capturing matching opportunities along the route when demand is too dispersed for effective pre-trip matching.
item.dc:creator: Yifan Shen, Junlin Chen, Julia Yan, Chiwei Yan

item.title: Debiasing optimal transport: classical and entropic
item.description: arXiv:2604.19981v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study the notion of debiasability for cost functions arising in optimal transport. We call a symmetric cost function $c:\mathscr{X}\times\mathscr{X}\to R\cup\{+\infty\}$ debiasable if it satisfies $c(x,y)\ge \tfrac{1}{2}c(x,x)+\tfrac{1}{2}c(y,y)$ for all $x,y\in\mathscr{X}$. Building on an equivalent characterization by an inf-representation $c(x,y)=\inf_{z\in\mathscr Z}\psi(x,z)+\psi(y,z)$ for some set $\mathscr Z$ and some function $\psi:\mathscr X\times\mathscr Z\to R\cup\{+\infty\}$, interpreted as a generalization of the midpoint identity for squared geodesic distances, we investigate the debiasability of costs defined on spaces of probability measures. Our primary focus is the entropic regularization of optimal transport across the different regimes of the regularization parameter $\varepsilon\in[0,+\infty]$, encompassing classical optimal transport ($\varepsilon=0$), entropic optimal transport ($\varepsilon>0$), and the Maximum Mean Discrepancy ($\varepsilon=+\infty$). For $\varepsilon\in(0,+\infty)$ we obtain debiasability under negative definiteness of the ground cost, through an explicit Gaussian factorization, and, more generally, under positive semidefiniteness of the kernel $e^{-c/\varepsilon}$ alone, conditions also proved necessary. All our results extend naturally to unbalanced optimal transport settings. Extending our factorizations to include a time parameter $t\in(0,1)$, we construct an entropic interpolation curve given by an intermediate measure $\eta_t\in\mathscr P(\mathscr Z)$ based on a barycentric formulation, which coincides with the marginals of the Schr\"odinger bridge between $\mu$ and $\nu$. As a byproduct, we derive a new proof for the entropic Benamou-Brenier formula under very mild assumptions.
item.dc:creator: Pierre-Cyril Aubin-Frankowski, Virginie Ehrlacher, Gabriele Todeschi

item.title: Approximate Dynamic Programming for Real-time Assignment of Extraboard Transit Operators
item.description: arXiv:2605.04511v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This study investigates real-time assignment decisions for extraboard transit operators, who are responsible for covering open work due to unexpected events such as driver absenteeism. Efficient usage of extraboard operators is critical as open work negatively affects service reliability. The problem is formulated as a Markov decision process, designed to capture its stochastic and sequential nature. Due to the problem's very large state space, an approximate policy is proposed in the form of an integer program, which maps a system state to assignment decisions such that the sum of immediate and expected future rewards is maximized. As part of off-line training, future value functions for individual operators are computed using a backward dynamic program. Then, the overestimation in the aggregate value obtained by summing individual values is corrected to account for the interaction among operators. Case studies are conducted based on the operations at a real-world transit agency. Key performance metrics including uncovered open work and extraboard utilization rates are examined for varying absenteeism rates and extraboard roster sizes. The approximate policy is shown to outperform benchmark decision rules mirroring real-world assignment strategies. Further numerical experiments are conducted to analyze different operational policies: (1) inclusion of overtime drivers in the reserve operator roster; (2) reward weights for work tasks that consider passenger wait time saved. Observations from these computational analyses provide actionable insights into extraboard sizing, overtime usage, and real-time dispatch practices at transit agencies.
item.dc:creator: Jilin Song, Amer Shalaby, Merve Bodur

item.title: Reachability-Augmented Dual Dynamic Programming for Optimal Path Parameterization
item.description: arXiv:2605.19089v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Optimal path parameterization (OPP) is a fundamental problem for planning trajectories along a prescribed geometric path under kinodynamic constraints and task-dependent objectives. Among existing OPP works, it remains challenging to simultaneously achieve feasibility guarantees, general-objective optimality certificates, and online-compatible computation in a unified framework, especially for third-order OPP (OPP3) with non-convex constraints. This paper proposes reachability-augmented dual dynamic programming (RDDP), a state-grid-free and objective-aware dynamic programming (DP) framework for OPP. The key idea is to replace the relatively complete recourse assumption used in classical dual DP (DDP) with OPP-specific backward reachable sets, and then generate both value-function cuts and trial trajectories only inside these reachable sets.
